passage.title: 'The Allotment in January', an unseen poem written for TGA
paras: Nothing grows here now. The beds lie
under a skin of frost, brown and folded
My father's spade leans on the shed,
its handle polished by thirty winters
of his hands. I lift it. It is heavier
than I remember, or I am lighter.
Still, I turn one row. The soil
breaks dark and sweet beneath the white,
and there, curled like a question,
going about the work of spring
as if no one had told it
that the man who dug here is gone.

questions.q: Annotate the poem (5 minutes): images, tone, structure, the turn.
questions.a: Annotations: frost 'skin' and unopened 'letters'; polished handle; 'heavier... or I am lighter'; 'Still' as the volta; the worm as continuing life; final line's plain statement of loss.
questions.model: Teacher annotates line 3 aloud: 'like letters nobody has opened': a simile linking the frozen beds to unread messages: things left unsaid with the father.

questions.q: in the portal response box, answer the question. Starter: 'The poet presents memory as...'
questions.a: Mark scheme points (AO2): frozen beds as unopened letters (unspoken words); the spade's polished handle as physical memory of the father; 'heavier... or I am lighter' (grief changes the speaker); the turn 'Still'; soil 'dark and sweet' and the worm 'curled like a question' as life continuing; enjambment pulling to the final line; three stanzas moving from stillness to action to quiet loss.
questions.model: Model opening shared after: 'The poet presents memory as something held in objects: the spade's handle is "polished by thirty winters / of his hands", so the father's absence is felt through the smoothness he left behind.'

questions.q: Compare your answer with the model points; add one missed point.
write one sentence on the effect of the final line.
questions.a: Its plain statement after the worm's 'work of spring' makes the loss land quietly and finally.
